entries.clue: Label meant to be edited? That’s very unfortunate (10)

indicators.note: an editor moves words about until they read better, so the letters are not left standing in the order the clue prints them

blocks.note: the ten letters of LABEL MEANT, resettled into a different word

annotation.walkthrough: The surface sells a printing job — a label with the wrong wording on it — and the sigh at the end is the only part of the sentence meant literally.
annotation.definitionFit: very unfortunate -> LAMENTABLE: something lamentable is bad enough to be worth lamenting, so the word measures misfortune by the grief it deserves.

entries.clue: No opening for bubbly host (4)

indicators.note: an opening is the way in at the front, so a word denied one starts a letter later than it should

blocks.note: barm is the froth on fermenting beer, so barmy first meant frothy

annotation.walkthrough: Barmy has drifted a long way: it began as a brewer's word and ended up meaning daft, and the surface's lively party-giver is nothing like the multitude wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: host -> ARMY: host is the old word for an armed multitude, kept alive in 'the Lord of hosts', so it names a great number under arms.

entries.clue: Component of toolbox routine took effect (5,3)

blocks.note: a drill is a fixed routine gone through again and again until it sticks
sanctions that bite are sanctions that work, so what bit took effect

annotation.walkthrough: 'Bit' as the past tense of bite is the step to spot: the clue never uses the word in its toolbox sense until the answer has already arrived.
annotation.definitionFit: Component of toolbox -> DRILL BIT: the bit is the cutting piece chucked into a drill, so it names a part of the kit, not the tool.

entries.clue: A measure of power taken up under old Canadian government? (6)

indicators.note: in a down entry what is taken up is read from the bottom, so those letters run the other way
a piece written under another sits below it on the page, so it follows in a down entry

blocks.note: O is the standing abbreviation for old
the watt is the measure of electrical power, and A WATT comes back the other way

annotation.walkthrough: Naming a capital for the government that sits in it is ordinary newspaper shorthand — Washington says, Ottawa announces — and the question mark is what licenses it.
annotation.definitionFit: Canadian government? -> OTTAWA: the city stands in for the administration housed there, the same metonymy that lets Westminster mean Parliament.

entries.clue: Oyster? Simple to swallow half of it (6)

indicators.note: what you swallow goes down inside you, so the letter is taken into the middle of the other word
split a two-letter word down the middle and one letter is left, and it is the back half that is wanted

blocks.note: naive is simple in the unworldly sense, and the word opens up after its first two letters
IT cut in half leaves a single T

annotation.walkthrough: Oysters are named for where they grew, so the home-grown ones are natives — the opening 'Oyster?' reads like an aside and is doing the whole job of the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Oyster? -> NATIVE: a native is the British-bred oyster of the Kent and Essex beds, so the question mark flags an example rather than a synonym.

entries.clue: Area amidst Northern university accommodation provoking illness (10)

indicators.note: whatever stands amidst two things stands between them, so this letter drops into the gap they leave

blocks.note: N is the compass abbreviation for northern
A is the standing abbreviation for area
U is the standing abbreviation for university
seating is what a hall accommodates its audience with

annotation.walkthrough: Three single-letter abbreviations in a row is what makes a ten-letter answer feel unreachable, right up until the last word of the wordplay hands over seven letters at once.
annotation.definitionFit: provoking illness -> NAUSEATING: nausea is the sick feeling itself, so what is nauseating brings it on rather than suffers it.

entries.clue: Study supporting Australian port (4)

indicators.note: a support holds something up from beneath, so in a down entry this piece is written below the other

blocks.note: A is the standing abbreviation for Australian
the small private room you shut yourself in to work

annotation.walkthrough: 'Study' is one of the crossword's hardest-worked words: DEN almost always, CON now and then, and hardly ever the act of studying.
annotation.definitionFit: port -> ADEN: Aden is the great harbour at the mouth of the Red Sea, so one named port stands in for the general word.

entries.clue: Suppressing anger is far more dispassionate (6)

indicators.note: to suppress a feeling is to hold it down out of sight, so those letters end up buried inside the word that keeps them

blocks.note: the little word FAR is the container, and it comes apart between its A and its R
ire is anger, three letters that turn up in crosswords far more often than in speech

annotation.walkthrough: The word doing the swallowing is the one you would read straight past — a three-letter adverb that looks like part of the definition and is really the wrapper.
annotation.definitionFit: more dispassionate -> FAIRER: fair here is the judge's sense, deciding without favour, so what is fairer is less swayed by feeling.

entries.clue: Source of drink and marijuana given to clubman? (3-5)

blocks.note: tea has been slang for marijuana since the jazz age
the caddy is the man who carries a golfer's clubs round the course

annotation.walkthrough: Both halves point at a gentleman's afternoon and mean something else: the drug rather than the leaf, the golf course rather than the club armchair.
annotation.definitionFit: Source of drink -> TEA-CADDY: the caddy is the box the leaves are kept in, so it is where the cup starts rather than the drink itself.

entries.clue: Oxide reliably breaking down (8)

indicators.note: a thing that breaks down comes apart into its pieces, and pieces can be put back together in another order

blocks.note: the eight letters of RELIABLY, rearranged

annotation.walkthrough: A chemistry answer with a one-word definition gives you nothing to guess at, so this is a clue to solve from the letters inwards rather than the meaning outwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Oxide -> BERYLLIA: beryllia is beryllium oxide, the hard white ceramic used where heat has to pass but current must not.

entries.clue: Cracked it, entering most of interior (6)

indicators.note: whatever enters a place ends up inside it, so these letters are planted within the ones the clue names next
most of a word is all but a little of it, and what gets left behind is the letter on the end

blocks.note: what is interior is inner, and the word arrives without its final letter
'it' is 1920s slang for sex appeal, which crosswords have written as SA ever since

annotation.walkthrough: SA for 'it' is worth learning outright: a person who had 'it' had sex appeal, and in a clue the pronoun almost never stands for the two letters I and T.
annotation.definitionFit: Cracked -> INSANE: cracked is the informal 'gone in the head', the same picture as a flaw running through something that ought to be sound.

entries.clue: About to leave road? Keep in place (4)

indicators.note: when something leaves it is no longer where it was, so those letters are gone from the word

blocks.note: a street is a road, and it is the word the wordplay works on
RE is about, as in 'Re: your letter' at the head of a memo

annotation.walkthrough: RE for 'about' is one of the two most-used pairs of letters in the crossword, and here the road surface and the printed page it really belongs to never meet.
annotation.definitionFit: Keep in place -> STET: stet is the proofreader's Latin for 'let it stand', the mark that cancels a correction and leaves the original wording alone.

entries.clue: One of a pair guided through river with hesitation (10)

indicators.note: something that goes through a thing passes into its middle, so these letters are driven in between the others

blocks.note: the Tweed runs along the Scottish border
to guide someone is to lead them
um is the noise of hesitating, and crosswords treat it as a word

annotation.walkthrough: Carroll's brothers are so alike that he needs both to make either one funny, which is what the definition is quietly telling you before you have a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: One of a pair -> TWEEDLEDUM: the Looking-Glass twins are never mentioned apart, so naming either one only ever names half of a matched set.

entries.clue: Book not generating interest or criticism (5)

blocks.note: B is the standing abbreviation for book
something lame falls flat and holds nobody's attention

annotation.walkthrough: 'Not generating interest' looks like a phrase off the financial pages and is a plain synonym — the money surface has nothing at all behind it.
annotation.definitionFit: criticism -> BLAME: blame is criticism with fault attached, saying not just that a thing went badly but whose doing it was.

entries.clue: Silent disease - no additional comment (3)

indicators.note: putting 'no' in front of a thing declares it absent, so those letters are struck out of the word

blocks.note: mumps is the swollen-glands illness of childhood
a PS is the extra line added once a letter has been signed off

annotation.walkthrough: The trick is noticing that two of the letters on the end of a childhood illness are themselves a word, and a word this clue has a definition for.
annotation.definitionFit: Silent -> MUM: to keep mum is to say nothing at all, the sense that survives in 'mum's the word'.

entries.clue: Hesitate to oust leader in state (4)

indicators.note: to oust someone is to turn them out of the place they held, so that letter is thrown clear of the word

blocks.note: to waver is to hesitate, swaying between two answers
the leader of WAVER is the letter at its head

annotation.walkthrough: AVER is a courtroom word — to assert something as fact — and it is one of that handful of short verbs that keep reappearing because their letters are so useful.
annotation.definitionFit: state -> AVER: to aver is to state something firmly and on the record, so the definition is the everyday verb for the formal one.

entries.clue: Voters cheer when Minister, ignoring leader, gets in (10)

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer a singular collective noun: an electorate is the whole body of voters counted as one thing, which is how newspapers use both words interchangeably.

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its head, and ignoring it means starting one letter late
whatever gets in has got inside, so these letters lodge in the middle of the others

blocks.note: to elate someone is to cheer them, and the word splits after its first two letters
a rector is a parish minister, arriving here without the R he starts with

annotation.walkthrough: 'Leader' means the letter at the head of a word rather than anybody in charge, and the election-night surface is there purely to stop you noticing that.
annotation.definitionFit: Voters -> ELECTORATE: the electorate is everyone entitled to cast a ballot, so the answer is the collective name for the people the definition lists.

entries.clue: Suggestion engineers should be brought in by city (6)

indicators.note: to be brought in by somebody is to be carried inside what they have, so these letters are set within the other word

blocks.note: Bath is the Somerset spa city, and it comes apart straight after its B
the Royal Engineers are RE, the sappers of the British Army

annotation.walkthrough: 'A breath of scandal' is the phrase the definition comes out of — a breath there is the faintest trace of a thing, nothing to do with lungs.
annotation.definitionFit: Suggestion -> BREATH: a breath of something is the merest hint of it, too slight to prove, which is exactly what a suggestion amounts to.

entries.clue: Good to avoid excessive clamour (3)

indicators.note: to avoid a thing is to keep well clear of it, so that letter is kept out of the word altogether

blocks.note: huge is excessive in size
G is the standing abbreviation for good

annotation.walkthrough: Hue and cry was a legal duty once: the shout that obliged every neighbour to join the chase. The clue wants that shout, not the colour.
annotation.definitionFit: clamour -> HUE: hue survives almost only in 'hue and cry', where it means the outcry itself rather than any shade of colour.

entries.clue: US state home to river touching the sea (6)

indicators.note: to be home to something is to have it living inside you, so this letter sits within the name that houses it

blocks.note: Maine is the state at the north-east corner of the US, and it opens after MA
R is the map abbreviation for river

annotation.walkthrough: The surface has a river reaching the coast and the wordplay has one letter inside a state, so 'home to' is doing hospitality above and plumbing below.
annotation.definitionFit: touching the sea -> MARINE: marine is the adjective for anything belonging to the sea, from marine life to marine insurance.

entries.clue: Lovers at it frenetically, increasingly under covers (8)

indicators.note: anything done frenetically is done without order, and letters handled that way do not stay as they were given
to go under covers is to be tucked out of sight beneath something, so these letters are buried inside the others

blocks.note: the four letters of AT IT, resettled and then opened up after the first
increasingly is more and more of a thing, so the word itself is more

annotation.walkthrough: Amoretti are the plump winged cupids of Italian painting, and the bedroom surface is the setter approaching the same subject from the least reverent end.
annotation.definitionFit: Lovers -> AMORETTI: the Italian plural means 'little loves', used both for cupids and, in the older English sense, for lovers themselves.

entries.clue: Sailor escaping bottom of ocean for a start (4)

indicators.note: what escapes gets clean away, so those letters are no longer among the ones left behind

blocks.note: the seabed is the floor of the ocean, one word and the whole of the raw material here
an AB is an able seaman, the crossword's default sailor

annotation.walkthrough: 'Bottom of ocean' is a definition of a word, not an instruction to take a last letter — spotting which of those it is decides whether the clue opens at all.
annotation.definitionFit: a start -> SEED: a seed is what a plant begins as, and the sense carries into 'the seeds of an idea' — a beginning still folded up.

entries.clue: Sauce a part of canapés today? (5)

indicators.note: only a part of what follows is wanted, so the answer is already sitting in those words rather than being built from them

blocks.note: canaPÉS TOday carries the answer straight across the gap between the two words

annotation.walkthrough: The join between the two words is where the eye slides past, and an accent sitting in the middle of the run makes it slide faster still.
annotation.definitionFit: Sauce -> PESTO: pesto is the Genoese pounding of basil, pine nuts, garlic and cheese, so one named sauce answers for the general word.

entries.clue: Possibly Afghan remains? Read more about that (6)

indicators.note: to go about a thing is to go round it, and 'that' points back at the remains the clue has just named

blocks.note: PTO — please turn over — is the note at the foot of a page telling you to read on
ash is what remains once a fire has burnt out

annotation.walkthrough: PTO is worth banking: three letters for a whole instruction, and one of the few abbreviations a setter can clue without naming a word at all.
annotation.definitionFit: Possibly Afghan -> PASHTO: Pashto is one of Afghanistan's two official languages, so 'Afghan' points at an example — Dari would have done as well.

entries.clue: Excellent US sports event not getting the bird? (6)

indicators.note: what you do not get you never have, so those letters never make it into the word at all

blocks.note: the Super Bowl is the NFL's championship game and the biggest American broadcast of the year
the owl is the bird, and it happens to be the end of the event's name

annotation.walkthrough: Getting the bird also means being booed off, so the phrase reads two ways in the surface while doing one plain job underneath.
annotation.definitionFit: Excellent -> SUPERB: superb sits at the top of the scale of praise, from the Latin superbus, proud — a clear step beyond good.

entries.clue: Kick-off of game upset spectators (4)

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer singular: the gate at a match is the crowd counted as one figure, which is why a paper reports 'a gate of forty thousand'.

indicators.note: a kick-off is the very start of a match, so only the starting letter of the word behind it is taken

blocks.note: the first letter of GAME, an ordinary initial hidden in football language
what ate at you is what upset you — 'what's eating him?' asks what is wrong

annotation.walkthrough: The gate of a match is both the crowd and the money they paid, named after the turnstile they came through rather than anything they did.
annotation.definitionFit: spectators -> GATE: a match's gate is its attendance, the paying crowd named by the entrance that counted them in.

entries.clue: Crowds, perhaps, having hour in river (6)

indicators.note: what is in a thing sits inside it, so these letters go among the ones the next word supplies

blocks.note: the Tees runs out to sea past Middlesbrough, and it opens after its first letter
hr is how a timetable abbreviates hour

annotation.walkthrough: Two's company, three's a crowd: that proverb is the whole of the definition, and 'perhaps' is there because only the proverb makes the equation true.
annotation.definitionFit: Crowds, perhaps -> THREES: the saying makes three a crowd, so 'perhaps' flags a definition that holds by proverb rather than by dictionary.

entries.clue: Expedition leaving South - what’s not to like? (4)

indicators.note: when a thing leaves it is gone from where it stood, so that letter drops out of the word

blocks.note: expedition is speed — 'with all expedition' means with all haste
S is the compass abbreviation for south

annotation.walkthrough: The polar journey in the surface is built on the sense of 'expedition' the clue does not use; the sense it does use is the one that means despatch.
annotation.definitionFit: not to like -> HATE: the definition arrives by negation, and hate is the strong opposite of liking rather than a mere absence of it.

entries.clue: Meadowlands contributing to unalloyed contentment (8)

indicators.note: what you contribute goes into the thing you contribute to, so these letters are dropped inside the other word

blocks.note: an unalloyed metal is pure, with nothing mixed into it, and the word splits after its P
a lea is a meadow, so leas are meadowlands

annotation.walkthrough: A lea is the poets' and place-namers' word for a meadow, and capitalising it turns it into somewhere in New Jersey for as long as the surface needs.
annotation.definitionFit: contentment -> PLEASURE: pleasure is settled enjoyment rather than a burst of delight, and that steadier sense is the one contentment shares.

entries.clue: Mollusc spurning new trip at sea (4)

indicators.note: to spurn a thing is to reject it outright, so that letter is turned away from the word

blocks.note: the snail is the shell-carrying mollusc of the garden
N is the standing abbreviation for new

annotation.walkthrough: 'At sea' belongs to the definition here — a sail is an outing on the water, not a piece of canvas — so the words that look like an instruction are the plain half.
annotation.definitionFit: trip at sea -> SAIL: 'we went for a sail' uses the noun taken straight off the verb, meaning the voyage rather than the canvas.

entries.clue: Impediment bringing in right horse at dressage? (8)

indicators.note: to bring something in is to fetch it inside, so this letter is carried into the middle of the word

blocks.note: a stutter is a speech impediment, and it opens up after its first two letters
R is the standing abbreviation for right

annotation.walkthrough: Dressage horses are judged on an exaggerated high-stepping walk, so the definition is a description and a joke in the same three words.
annotation.definitionFit: horse at dressage? -> STRUTTER: a strutter is anything that struts, and the showy high step of dressage is exactly that, so the question mark flags an example.

entries.clue: Charlie, slowly, finally absorbing section of convoluted story? (6)

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and the definition a noun phrase: read it as 'of convoluted story', with the question mark licensing the shorthand of naming the thing described.

indicators.note: what is absorbed is taken up inside, so this letter is drawn into the middle of the others

blocks.note: a right Charlie is a fool, and so is a twit
slowlY ends on this letter
S is the standing abbreviation for section

annotation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' is the fool of 'a proper Charlie', not the NATO letter C the surface is hoping you reach for first.
annotation.definitionFit: convoluted story? -> TWISTY: a twisty plot keeps doubling back on itself, which is what convoluted describes — a route with too many turns to follow straight.
